For some a half-mora, for others an atom: The letter "m" becomes anusvara before "r", sibilants and "h", and even before a suffix; before labials it becomes the homorganic nasal, and before stops, the final one.
When a word ends in "n" and a vowel follows, they call the "a" coloured (nasalised); it is coloured by the "t"-sound.
When the preceding word ends in "n" and consonants like "y, v, h" follow, the half-mora of the former is coloured with an atom-mora.
The final "n" joined with a vowel is made with the fourth; "r", "ranga", and elision, or with anusvara, sometimes.
Ranga rises from the heart, joined with a bell-metal sound, soft and two moras long; "dadhanvan" is an example.
As a woman of Saurashtra says "aram", so the ranga should be used; this is my (Narada's) view.
The vowels, the letters "ga, da, da, ba," "n, n, n, m" with the sibilants — ten are declared as word-finals for the four kinds of words.
Tone is high, low, and svarita; where consonants do not occur, there the vowel stands.
The teachers hold the threefold tone to be vowel-dominant. Know the consonant as a jewel, and the vowel as the thread.
As a strong king seizes the realm of a weak one, so a strong vowel should seize a weak consonant.
Both "ubha" and "vivritti", "sha, sha, sa", and "r", the root of the tongue and upadhmaniya — the movement of the sibilants is eightfold.
Where vowel and suffix are open in the conjunction (samhita), there it is regarded as visarga, and a palatal arises.
In a diphthong, in the following junction, if "y" and "v" have fallen asleep, the consonant-named openness is the vowel-named re-combination.
Where a sibilant ends and pauses and some chance arises, the openness there should be called vowel-named.
If a word follows with "r" and the rest after a junction of "ya" and "ubha", know it as ending in a vowel, otherwise a sibilant is manifest.
The first and last letters at word-ends, if they have reached the second place, with "sha, sha, sa" as suffixes,
should be shown as though the firsts joined with sibilants were seconds. Do not take them so, as in "matsya", "kshura", "apsara".
Metre-measure, rhythm, and foot-place are the three reasons; verses are of their own free rhythm, and feet are by syllable-count.
One should determine the rik-word vowels and svarabhakti by the metre-measure; "pratyayeta sa harepham" he measures with svarabhakti.
In the sound "ri" the "r" is separate and the suffix would be in vain; know the short "ri" if joined with a sibilant.
Where "ri" joined only with a sibilant is pressed, know it as a heavy syllable; here "trcham" is an example.
Rishabham, "grihitam", "Brihaspatim", "prithivyam", "nirriti" — in these five there are "ri" sounds, without doubt.
Before "sha, sha, sa, ha" and "r", svarabhakti arises at the junction of two words, sometimes lacking "i" and "u", sometimes without a single word's sequence.
Svarabhakti is said to be twofold: in "ri" and in "r" — vowel-initial and consonant-initial, as thought by those who consider syllables.
In the sibilants, vowel-initial; in "ha", consonant-initial; they know it open in the sibilants and closed in "ha".
Using svarabhakti, one should avoid faults of "sri"; also "i", "u", and devoured faults likewise.
Followed by a conjunct, followed by "cha", visarjaniya, two-mora; then "santika", "n", "m" with anusvara, and "ghuta".
A verse whose first foot has twelve moras and third also; the second is eighteen, and it has attained fifteen moras; one whose mark is stated, the other is called "vipula".
If a short syllable is not followed by a conjunct, it is short; know the long ones as those followed by a conjunct.
Where an opening is seen standing before a svara-syllable,
know it as a heavy tone; kshaipra is not there. The marks of tone of words are to be known as eightfold.
Final-udatta, initial-udatta, udatta, anudatta, low-svarita, middle-udatta, svarita, double-udatta — these are the eight names of words.

Agnih, "somah", "pro vo viryam", "havisha", "svar", "vanaspatih" — examples. Between... what follows after svarita, the syllables of the stream of pracaya; all pracaya-stationed ones: the pre-udatta is struck.
Where pracaya is seen, the wise should strike the tone; where svarita alone stands, he should lower it softly.
The teacher's fivefold: name, ease, placing, production, assertion, utterance. Here it is said: for a syllable whose production is not obtained, assertion is to be carried; that is its grammar.
Tumburu, Bhavad, Vishvavasu and other Gandharvas do not know the Sama production hidden in the subtlety of tone.
One should always guard the fire of the belly... (a passage on digestion and rising before dawn; text unclear).
Rising is approved before dawn, after the autumn equinox, as long as the middle night of spring lasts.
Rising in the morning in silence, he should chew a tooth-twig of mango, palasha, bilva, apamarga or shirisha.
Khadira, kadamba, karavira and karanja — all thorny, milky, meritorious and famous trees.
By this subtlety and sweetness arise in his production, and he forms the letters well, as the ancient eastern way.
A student should always eat the triphala with salt; this kindles fire and intelligence and refines voice and letters.
Having done the necessary duties and attended to the belly, having drunk honey and ghee, and being pure, he should then speak.
He should begin first in the low register; this is the rule in all branches. Passing seven mantras, he may let his voice go as he wishes.
He should not force the voice, nor obstruct the breath; by obstructing breath, a bad voice arises; the sweetness of voice and consonants is lost, without doubt.
What comes from a bad ford, burnt and eaten by wrong letters — he has no release, as from the sin of a snake-bite.
What comes from a good ford, memorised, well-established, uttered with a good voice from one's own mouth — Brahman shines; not one who is sing-song, thick-lipped, or wholly nasal.
One who stammers or has a bound tongue is not fit to speak the recitations.
With a single mind, inwardly restrained, bathed, and free of song, he should apply the letters whose teeth and lips are fine.
Fierce, stubborn men, the lazy and the sick, and those whose minds wander, do not grasp the five sciences.
Slowly learning, slowly wealth, slowly climbing a mountain, slowly travelling roads, one should not go more than a yojana.
An ant travels a thousand yojanas slowly; Garuda, not moving, does not go one step.
Speech struck by sin cannot speak the recitations, like the talk of a deaf man, though a clever woman looks on.
One who studies in a whisper, as if frightened, remains in doubt among a thousand forms.
What is learned from a book and not in the presence of a teacher does not shine in an assembly, like a woman pregnant by a paramour.
Seeing the wearing away of eye-ointment and the heap of an anthill, one should make the day fruitful in giving and study.
The great anthill made by insects with fine dust: there strength is not the cause, but effort.
Learning multiplied a thousandfold is hundredfold praised; it will come to the tip of the tongue like water to a low place.
As of well-bred horses who sleep half the night, sleep does not stay long in the eyes of those seeking learning.
One should not be slow at meals, nor bound by women; a seeker of learning would cross even the ocean like Garuda or a swan.
Afraid of crowds like a snake, of company like hell, and of women like demonesses — such a one attains learning.
The deceitful do not gain their ends, nor eunuchs, the proud, noisy, wretched, or those who wait on their own ease.
As by a digging tool a man finds water in the earth, so the one who serves a teacher obtains the learning he holds.
Learning comes by service to the teacher, or with abundant wealth, or learning for learning; not otherwise.
Learning without service, even if it comes with qualities of intellect, is like a young barren woman — it is not fruitful for him.
Thus the text on Shiksha has been given to you in outline; knowing the first of the Vedangas, one becomes fit to be Brahman.
(Describing the ill effects of planets:) He mounts for desire a meat-eater's animal; he lives with the lowest-born, asses and camels...
Even travelling he thinks himself followed by others; he is dejected, his undertakings fail, and he sinks without cause.
Afflicted by that, a prince does not get a kingdom, a girl no husband, a woman no child, a teacher no learned status, a pupil no learning;
a merchant no profit, a farmer no harvest. For him a bath is to be performed on an auspicious day by rule, with white mustard paste, and blessings pronounced by the twice-born.
Earth from a horse-stable, elephant-stable, anthill, confluence and lake, and rochana, perfumes and guggulu, should be quickly put in.
Four pots brought from the lake by vessels of one colour; on a red bull's hide he should be seated on a good seat.
Thousand-eyed, hundred-streamed, purified by sages — with it I sprinkle you; may the purifying ones purify you.
May King Varuna give you fortune, the Sun, Brihaspati, Indra, Vayu and the Seven Sages.
Whatever ill-fortune is in your hair, parting, head, forehead, ears, eyes, may the waters always drive away.
With mustard oil for the bath, with a ladle of udumbara he should offer on the head with kusha, held with the left hand.
Mita, Sammita, Shalakatankata, Kushmanda and Rajaputra — with these names ending in "svaha"...
with names, bali-mantras and salutations, he should give at a crossroads, at the sun, spreading kusha all around.
Cooked and uncooked rice, a sesame-rice dish, fish cooked and raw, meat — as much as these.
Flowers of many kinds, fragrance, and liquor of the three kinds, radish, pastries and cakes, and garlands of ota (hemp?).
Curd-rice, milk-rice, jaggery-and-flour sweets: having brought all of these and bowed his head to the ground,
he should approach Ambika, mother of Vinayaka, offering a full handful of water with durva, mustard and flowers.
Give me beauty, give me fame, give me fortune, O Goddess; give me sons, give me wealth, give me all desires.
Having approached Shiva, Durga and Uma's lord, he should worship with incense, ghee-lamps, offerings, perfume, garlands and ointments.
Then, clothed in white, with white garlands and ointments, he should feed Brahmins and also give his teacher a pair of garments.
Having thus worshipped Vinayaka, he should worship the planets — one desiring prosperity, peace, nourishment, long life and vigour.
Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Rahu and Ketu — these nine planets are to be established in order.
They should be made of copper, silver, red sandal, gold, gold, silver, iron, lead, for good fortune.
Or drawn on cloth in their own colours, or in diagrams with perfumes; garments and flowers should be given in the colour of each.
Perfumes, offerings, incense and guggulu should be given; and oblations with mantras for each deity should be prepared.
The mantras: "Akrishnena", "Imam deva", "Agnir murdha divah kakut", "Udbudhyasva", "Yad arya", and "Annat parisrutah".
Shanno devih, then from the section, "Ketum krinvann aketave".
Arka, palasha, khadira, apamarga, pippala, udumbara, shami, durva and kusha are the fuel sticks, in order.
One hundred and eight, or twenty-eight, of each should be offered with honey and ghee, or with curd or milk.
Jaggery-rice, milk-rice, havishya (pure sacrificial food), milk preparations, rice with milk, curd-rice, flour offerings, meat and variegated food —
the wise should give these to Brahmins as food in the order of the planets, as able, as obtained, honoured, by rule.
A cow, a conch, a bull, a garment, a horse, a black cow, gold, iron, a goat — these are remembered as the fees (for each planet).
Whatever substance belongs to each, by that he should be worshipped with his own fee. O Brahmin, a boon has been given to them: "Worshipped, you will honour."
The wealth, class and rise of kings depend on the planets, as do the existence and non-existence of the world; therefore the planets are most to be worshipped.
Worship of the Sun always, the lord's tilaka, and of Mahaganapati — doing these one attains success.
He attains fruitfulness of his deeds and unsurpassed prosperity.
One who begins worship of the planets without having done the worship of the Mothers — the Mothers are angry with him and create obstacles.
Having arranged the Vasor-dhara with the Vasu purifying mantra, the Mothers beginning with Gauri are to be worshipped in auspicious rites by those wishing welfare.
Gauri, Padma, Shachi, Medha, Savitri, Vijaya, Jaya, Devasena, Svadha, Svaha, Matrika, Dhriti,
Pushti, Hrishti, Tushti, with the family deity and Ganesha — these sixteen are to be worshipped at times of increase.
Invocation, water for the feet, welcome water, bath, sandal, whole rice-grains, flowers, incense, lamp, fruits,
food, rinsing water, betel and areca, waving of lights and the fee — in this order they should be offered for satisfaction.
I shall tell the ancestral rite, which increases wealth and progeny. New moon, eighth days, increase (vriddhi), the two courses and the dark fortnight,
a gift, the acquisition of Brahmins, the equinox, the sun's transit, the Vyatipata, the elephant's shadow, eclipses of moon and sun,
and one's own inclination — these are declared the times of shraddha. The best in all Vedas: a Vedic scholar, a knower of Brahman,
a knower of Vedic meaning, a reciter of Jyeshtha-Sama, Trimadhu, Trisuparna, a sister's son, priest, son-in-law, sacrificer, father-in-law, maternal uncle,
Trinachiketa, daughter's son, disciple, relatives, kinsmen, those devoted to rites, devoted to austerity, keepers of the five fires, celibates,
and those devoted to father and mother — Brahmins are the wealth of shraddha. A sick man, one with deficient or excess limbs, a one-eyed man, a son of a remarried woman,
one who has broken the vow, a son by adultery (kunda, golaka), one with bad nails, black teeth, a hired teacher, an impotent man, a defiler of a maiden, one falsely accused,
a friend-betrayer, slanderer, seller of soma, one who marries before his elder brother, abandoner of mother, father and teacher, one who eats the food of a kunda, son of a Shudra woman,
one who is another's husband first, a thief, and those fallen from their duties are censured. The self-controlled, pure man should invite Brahmins the day before.
They too should be restrained in mind, speech and body. In the afternoon, having honoured them with welcome as they arrive,
holding a purifier in hand, having sipped water, he should seat them on seats: Brahmins for the gods as able, and an odd number for the ancestors.
In a pure place, sloping to the south, supplied by another: two for the gods facing east, three for the ancestors facing north, or even one each.
The same for the maternal grandfathers' line, or the Vaishvadeva there. Giving water for washing hands and kusha for seats,
with permission he should invite with the verse "Vishvedevasa...", scatter barley, and in a vessel with a purifier,
pouring water with "Shanno devih", barley with "Yavo 'si", and with the mantra "Ya divya..." he should put foot-water in the hand.
Having given water, perfume, garlands, food with a lamp, he should then do it from the left, circumambulating the ancestors.
Giving double kusha, he invokes the ancestors with "Ushantas tva...", and with their permission chants "Ayantu nah".
Sesame to be used in place of barley, he should do the water offering and the rest as before; having given the offering with barley in the vessel by rule,
with "Pitribhyah sthanam asi" he places the vessel inverted, and when about to do it in the fire he asks for the ghee-soaked food.
Permitted by "Do it", he offers in the fire as at the ancestral sacrifice; he gives the remains of the offering attentively in the vessels.
In what is obtained and especially in what is to be hidden, having given the food, he addresses the vessel, "The vessel of earth..."
With "Idam Vishnuh" he places the Brahmin's thumb in the food; with the Gayatri and the vyahritis and the three verses "Madhu vata..."
having chanted, they may speak as they like; they eat silently. He should give food, liked and fit for offerings, without anger or haste.
When they are satisfied, having chanted the purifiers and the earlier chant, taking the food: "You are satisfied", and approving the remainder,
he should scatter that food on the ground and give water once each. Taking all the food with sesame, facing south,
near the leavings he should give rice-balls as in the ancestral sacrifice; so too for the maternal grandfathers; then give sipping water.
Then the blessing, then the imperishable water; giving the fee as able, he should utter "svadha".
Permitted by "Let it be said", "svadha" is said for those honoured; when they say "Astu svadha", he should sprinkle water on the ground.
May the Vishvedevas be pleased — when the Brahmins say so, he chants this: "May our givers prosper, the Vedas and progeny,
may faith not leave us, may we have much to give." Having said this with pleasant words, he bows and dismisses them.
With "Vaje vaje", with pleasure, the dismissal is first of the ancestors. In the vessel where they were first placed as offering...
making the ancestors' vessel upright, he should dismiss the Brahmins, follow them in circumambulation, and eat what the ancestors have partaken.
He should be celibate that night with the Brahmins. Thus by circumambulation, at a time of increase, he should honour the Nandimukha ancestors
with rice-balls made of barley mixed with curd and jujube. Ekoddishta is without the gods, with one offering-vessel and one purifier,
without invocation, fire-offering and "karana", in the left-handed way. "May it be imperishable" at the place, and at the dismissal of Brahmins,
he says "Be pleased"; they reply, "We are pleased." He should make four vessels of perfumed water with sesame.
For the offering water he should pour the water of the deceased's vessel into the ancestors' vessels; with the two verses "Ye samanah"; the rest as before.
This is the sapindikarana, the ekoddishta of women too. If the sapindikarana is done before the year ends for someone,
for him too, food with a water-pot should be given to a Brahmin for a year. On the day of death monthly should be done, for a year,
then yearly, and in the eleventh month on the day. He should give the balls to a goat, cow or Brahmins, or into fire or water.
He should cast it among good Brahmins; he should not wipe away the Brahmin's leavings. With havishya food for a month, with milk-rice for a year,
with fish, deer, ram, bird, goat and spotted-deer flesh, and with the meat of the eni, ruru, boar and hare, in order (as prescribed for each month).
